title: Students Report By Geography
statement:
One table lists students and where they come from:

- `Student(name, continent)`: one row per student. `continent` is one of `'America'`, `'Asia'` or `'Europe'`. The table has no key and may hold duplicate rows; each copy is a separate student. America has at least as many students as Asia and at least as many as Europe.

Pivot the table into three columns named `America`, `Asia` and `Europe`, in that order. Each column lists the names of that continent's students sorted alphabetically, one name per row: row 1 holds the alphabetically first name of every continent, row 2 the second, and so on. When a continent runs out of names, its cell is `null`. Return the rows in this position order (row 1 first); there are as many rows as America has students.
constraints: America has at least as many students as Asia and as Europe
Within a continent, no two names differ only in letter case
reference:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, continent,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY continent ORDER BY name) AS position
  FROM Student
)
SELECT
  MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'America' THEN name END) AS America,
  MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'Asia' THEN name END) AS Asia,
  MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'Europe' THEN name END) AS Europe
FROM ranked
GROUP BY position
ORDER BY position;
brute:
WITH RECURSIVE america AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM Student WHERE continent = 'America'
),
slots (k) AS (
  SELECT 1 FROM america WHERE n > 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.k + 1 FROM slots AS s, america AS a WHERE s.k < a.n
),
reach AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT s.continent, s.name,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Student AS t WHERE t.continent = s.continent AND t.name <= s.name) AS upto
  FROM Student AS s
)
SELECT
  (SELECT MIN(r.name) FROM reach AS r WHERE r.continent = 'America' AND r.upto >= slots.k) AS America,
  (SELECT MIN(r.name) FROM reach AS r WHERE r.continent = 'Asia' AND r.upto >= slots.k) AS Asia,
  (SELECT MIN(r.name) FROM reach AS r WHERE r.continent = 'Europe' AND r.upto >= slots.k) AS Europe
FROM slots
ORDER BY slots.k
notes:
## Intuition

The output puts names from different rows of `Student` side by side, so each name needs a coordinate: its column is its continent, and its row is its position in the continent's alphabetical list. `ROW_NUMBER()` partitioned by continent and ordered by name gives exactly that position. Once every name has a (position, continent) coordinate, grouping by position and picking the one name per continent with conditional aggregation turns the long table into the wide one.

## Approach

1. CTE `ranked`: every student with `position = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY continent ORDER BY name)`. Duplicates get consecutive positions, so each copy has its own row.
2. `GROUP BY position`: one output row per position.
3. In each group, `MAX(CASE WHEN continent = '...' THEN name END)` picks the single name of that continent, or `null` when the continent has fewer students. One such column per continent, named `America`, `Asia`, `Europe`.
4. `ORDER BY position` lists the rows in alphabetical position order.

## Example 1, step by step

- `ranked`: America gets Jack → 1 and Jane → 2; Asia gets Xi → 1; Europe gets Pascal → 1.
- Position 1 holds Jack, Xi and Pascal, one per continent, so the row is `(Jack, Xi, Pascal)`.
- Position 2 holds only Jane; Asia and Europe have nothing there, so the row is `(Jane, null, null)`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for n students to sort within each continent, then one pass to group by position.
- Space: O(n) for `ranked`.

## Pitfalls

- `RANK()` or `DENSE_RANK()` gives duplicate names the same position, and `MAX` then folds them into one cell, losing a student; `ROW_NUMBER()` keeps them apart.
- Forgetting `PARTITION BY continent` numbers all students together, so names of different continents never share a row.
- `MAX` is only a way to pick the one non-null value in a group; it is not choosing the "largest" name. Without the `CASE`, it would mix continents.
- Leaving out `ORDER BY position` returns the rows in whatever order the grouping produced.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ranked` | each student with its alphabetical `position` within its continent |
| `position` | the output row a name belongs to |
| `MAX(CASE ...)` | the name of one continent at this position, or `null` |
| `America`, `Asia`, `Europe` | the three pivoted columns |

narration.1: The CTE gives every student a coordinate inside their continent.
narration.3: ROW_NUMBER restarts at 1 for each continent and counts names alphabetically, giving duplicates separate positions.
narration.7: In each position group, the CASE keeps only the America name and MAX picks it out (null if there is none).
narration.8: The same pattern fills the Asia column.
narration.11: One output row per alphabetical position.
narration.12: Rows come out in position order, so each column reads alphabetically from top to bottom.
